This implies that Thiothixene may exert its pharmacological effects through a mechanism similar to those of its structural relatives. The lowest common ancestor of Thiothixene and Acepromazine, which is an agent affecting the nervous system, suggests a potential role in modulating neural activity, possibly through interactions with ion channels or transporters. The binding of Acepromazine to Slc22a1, a gene involved in ion transport, further supports the hypothesis that Thiothixene may influence Slc22a1 through a similar mechanism, possibly by affecting ion homeostasis. The integration of these relationships highlights a possible dependency on Slc22a1, which could be critical for the pharmacological effects of Thiothixene.
